title: Demyelinating Optic Neuritis & Neuro-Ophthalmology Essentials
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of demyelinating optic nerve diseases, including Multiple Sclerosis, NMOSD, and infectious variants. It details diagnostic markers, treatment regimens, and long-term prognostic factors.

branches: Normally myelinated nerve fibres lose insulating myelin layer
Myelin is phagocytosed by microglia and macrophages
Astrocytes lay down fibrous tissue in plaques
Disrupts nervous conduction within white matter tracts (brain, brainstem, spinal cord)

sections.title: Major Demyelinating Conditions
content: Isolated optic neuritis: No initial clinical evidence of generalized demyelination (though high proportion subsequently develop it).
Multiple sclerosis (MS): By far the most common demyelinating disease.
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD): Previously Devic disease; rare autoimmune disease.
MOG antibody disorder (MOGAD): Recently identified rare autoimmune disease.
Schilder disease: Very rare relentlessly progressive generalized disease.

sections.title: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD)
sections.content: NMOSD involves antibodies against aquaporin 4 protein in astrocyte cell membranes. It typically affects middle-aged women but can occur at any age. Characterized by bilateral optic neuritis and long-segment transverse myelitis (spinal cord demyelination) within a few weeks. Most patients have repeated attacks separated by remission. The NMO-IgG blood test is highly specific and positive in 70% of patients. Acute treatment: high-dose IV steroids, followed by oral steroids; if ineffective, plasmapheresis. Long-term: immunosuppressive drugs. Recently approved for anti-aquaporin positive adults: Eculizumab, inebilizumab, and satralizumab.

sections.title: MOGAD & Schilder Disease
content: MOGAD: Antibodies form against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG); results in inflammation of optic nerve and spinal cord; bilateral simultaneous optic neuropathy is common.
Schilder Disease: Onset prior to age 10; death within 1–2 years; bilateral optic neuritis without improvement may occur.

sections.title: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Overview
content: Idiopathic demyelinating disease of CNS white matter.
Infection with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) significantly increases risk (though not sufficient alone).
More common in women than men.
Presentation: Typically 3rd–4th decades; usually relapsing/remitting pattern (may switch to unremitting later); less commonly progressive from outset.

sections.title: Clinical Features of Demyelinating Optic Neuritis
content: Symptoms: Subacute monocular visual impairment; usual age 20–50 years (mean ~30).
Phosphenes: Tiny white or coloured flashes or sparkles.
Pain: Present in >90%; exacerbated by ocular movement; may precede/accompany visual loss; lasts a few days.
Other Symptoms: Frontal headache and tenderness of the globe.
Signs: VA usually 6/18–6/60 (rarely worse); impaired colour vision; Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD).
Disc Appearance: Normal in 2/3 (retrobulbar neuritis); 1/3 show papillitis (Fig 19.8).
Fellow Eye: Temporal disc pallor may indicate previous optic neuritis.

rows: Vision worsens over several days to 3 weeks
Initial recovery rapid; then slower over 6-12 months
TIP: MS-related ON usually improves without treatment over months
Weakness, stiffness, sphincter disturbance, sensory loss
Lhermitte sign (neck flexion shock), Uhthoff phenomenon (heat/exercise worsening)
Common: Retrobulbar ON, Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, Nystagmus. Uncommon: Skew deviation, Ocular motor nerve palsies. Rare: Uveitis, Periphlebitis

sections.title: Investigations in Multiple Sclerosis
content: Lumbar Puncture: Oligoclonal bands on CSF protein electrophoresis in 90–95%.
MRI: Changes in optic nerve (STIR imaging) and characteristic white matter plaques (supratentorial/corpus callosum).
VEPs: Abnormal (conduction delay, reduced amplitude) in up to 100% of clinically definite MS.

sections.title: Risk of Developing MS Post-Optic Neuritis
Predictors of Lower MS Risk
content: Male gender
Absence of preceding viral syndrome
Negative test for EBV
Presence of optic disc swelling, disc/peripapillary haemorrhages, or macular exudates
Vision reduced to No Light Perception (NLP)
Absence of periocular pain

sections.title: MS Statistics & Genetics
content: Optic neuritis is the presenting feature of MS in up to 30%.
ON occurs in 50% of established MS patients.
Not hereditary, but higher probability in close relatives.
Association with HLA DR15 and DQ6.

sections.title: Indications for Steroid Treatment in ON
content: Start treatment within 48 hours for potential axon preservation and VA improvement.
If VA is worse than 6/12 in week 1: speeds recovery by 2–3 weeks and delays clinical MS short-term.
IV Regimen: Methylprednisolone sodium succinate 1g daily (250mg 6-hourly) for 3 days.
Oral Regimen: Prednisolone (1mg/kg daily) for 11 days, followed by 3-day taper.
Warning: Oral prednisolone alone may increase recurrence risk if used without prior IV steroids.

rows: 1a/1b variants; early stage use; subcutaneous/intramuscular; flu-like symptoms; good long-term safety.
Subcutaneous; reduces relapse/progression; 'decoy' action; injection site reaction in 1/3.
Monoclonal antibody for highly active relapsing-remitting MS; reduces relapses by 2/3; systemic side effects.
Helpful for highly active and primary progressive disease; rare risk of fatal PML (leukoencephalopathy).
Potentially most cost-effective due to dosing strategy; used in difficult cases.
Cladribine, fingolimod, mitoxantrone (used for active/highly active relapsing MS).

sections.title: Prognosis & Management Strategy
content: Prognosis: >90% recover VA to 6/9 or better. Colour vision/RAPD may stay abnormal. Temporal pallor or atrophy may ensue.
Chronic ON: ~10% develop stepwise/progressive loss.
Relapse: 80-85% of MS patients experience relapses.
Approach: Multidisciplinary. First attack = Steroids + IFNβ/Glatiramer. Progressive MS = Ocrelizumab.

rows: Post-viral (measles, mumps, rubella, etc.) or post-immunization. Common in children. Bilateral papillitis/neuroretinitis. Good prognosis.
Unilateral loss, severe headache, spheno-ethmoidal sinusitis. Spread of infection/vasculitis. Rx: Antibiotics/Drainage.
Bartonella henselae; cat scratch/bite; causes neuroretinitis.
Borrelia burgdorferi (tick bite); neuroretinitis or retrobulbar neuritis; mimics MS.
Associated with AIDS and meningitis; can be bilateral.
Spread from retinitis (ARN/PORN) or HZO; common in immunocompromised.

content.explanation: Bilateral severe visual loss 1-3 weeks after viral infection is common in children; however, the prognosis for visual recovery is good.
